rv.q: By all things holy, this is a very busy production; it’s cacophonous and fidgety, occasionally ingenious, often absurd.
At times it feels wilfully incoherent – though much about it is compelling.
Ambitious but incoherent, it's a show that embraces some of the good as well as the unfortunate meanings of 'diabolical'.
Lloyd and Teevan are astute about today's slavish fixation with celebrity, yet the result feels like an exercise in bombarding us with toxic images.

There's nothing intrinsically wrong with this sort of star-driven "event" theatre...But alas there's little that's intrinsically right about Jamie Lloyd's revival, which...verges on being totally incomprehensible in this dismally conceived rehash...Harington's own status perhaps adds another level of in-jokeyness or insight to proceedings...It...

Colin Teevan replaces Marlowe’s unappetising middle section with some incoherent satire. The stage gibbers with spirits writhing around in grubby knickers. Jenna Russell is an acid, wheedling Mephistopheles, who provides an uplifting rendition of Bat out of Hell.
The production is certainly not shy about finding excuses to strip Harington almost naked, right down to his blood-stained jockey shorts.
However, like the magic tricks bestowed on its soul-selling protagonist, it’s rather more flash than substance.
At best, it’s a headrush; at worst, a headache — a jumble of depression and suicide, celebrity cults and Internet culture that means this Faustus fails to cohere.
A fine actor, she seems at sea in this rudderless show; it pains me to say it, but the best bit is her interval entertainment, where she belts out a karaoke version of "Bat out of Hell".
I doubt if I’ve ever seen a classic play mounted with so little connection to its original text.
After enduring Jamie Lloyd's modern version of Christopher Marlowe's 16th-century play, I'm convinced it is a case of 'better the devil you know'.
Kit Harington bares his bottom but just survives this farrago which makes Irvine Welsh seem like Terence Rattigan. Utter drivel.

cn.t: Lloyd's graphic, celebrity-focused update divides critics: some find Kit Harington's star turn and flashy spectacle engaging, but most dismiss the production as superficial shock tactics that sacrifices substance for style.
